cues.en: Tonight, I'd like to tell you about one of the big questions in science. It's a question that goes back at least two and a half thousand years to the ancient Greeks, and it's a question that has been discussed in this room many, many times over the past 200 years, but it's an important question, and I think it's important that we revisit it. And the question is simply this. It's, what are we made of?
cues.zh: 今晚，我想和大家聊聊科学界的一个重大问题。这个问题至少可以追溯到两千五百年前的古希腊，在过去的两百年里，它也在这个房间里被讨论过无数次，但它至关重要，我认为我们有必要再次重温。这个问题其实很简单，那就是：我们究竟是由什么构成的？

cues.en: What are the fundamental building blocks of nature that you and me and everything else in the universe are constructed from? That's the story I'd like to tell. So what I'd like to do is try and give you an overview of our current understanding. I'd also like to try and give you an overview of where we hope to go in the future, of what progress we can hope to make in the next few years and few decades.
cues.zh: 构成你、我和宇宙万物的自然基本构件究竟是什么？这就是我想讲述的故事。因此，我希望能为大家梳理一下我们目前的认知。同时，我也想展望一下未来的方向，看看在接下来的几年和几十年里，我们有望取得哪些进展。

cues.en: And we're going to cover quite a lot of ground in this talk. I should warn you now. Not least because I'm going to discuss every single thing in the universe, quite literally. We're going to talk amongst other things about what's happening at the world's most powerful particle collider. This is a machine that's called the Large Hadron Collider, or the LHC for short. It'll come up a lot in this talk. And it's a machine which is based underground in a place called CERN, which is just outside Geneva.
cues.zh: 先提醒大家一下，今晚我们要讲的内容非常多。这不仅仅是因为从字面意义上讲，我要探讨宇宙中的万事万物。除其他内容外，我们还将讨论在世界上最强大的粒子对撞机上发生的事情。这台机器被称为大型强子对撞机，简称 LHC。今晚它会频繁登场。这是一台建在地下的机器，位于日内瓦城外的 CERN。

cues.en: We'll also talk about experiments in the last few years that look backwards in time towards the Big Bang that give us some understanding about what was happening in the first few fractions of a second after time itself started to exist. And on top of all this, I also want to give you some idea about
cues.zh: 我们还将探讨近些年来那些回溯时间、望向大爆炸的实验，它们让我们得以了解在时间诞生后的最初极短瞬间里究竟发生了什么。除此以外，我还想让大家领略一下

cues.en: the theoretical, abstract ideas, and even a little bit of an idea about the mathematics that underlies our current understanding of the universe. Because I'm a theoretical physicist. What I do is study the equations, try to understand the equations that govern the world we live in, and so I'd just like to give you a flavor of what that's about. At some point, I should warn you now, at some point, I'm even going to show you an equation.
cues.zh: 那些理论性的、抽象的概念，甚至稍微了解一下支撑我们目前对宇宙认知的数学知识。因为我是一名理论物理学家。我的工作就是研究这些方程，尝试去理解主宰我们这个世界的方程，所以我希望能让大家感受一下那是什么样的体验。我得先提醒各位，在讲座的某个时刻，我甚至会给大家展示一个方程。

cues.en: OK. You know that you can get sent on training courses for this kind of thing. There's a number one rule. The number one rule is never show them any equations. If you show them equations, you'll just terrify them. At some point in this lecture, you're all going to be terrified. So just prepare yourselves. OK. OK.
cues.zh: 好吧。大家都知道做科普演讲是受过培训的，其中有一条头号法则。这条头号法则就是：绝对不要给观众看任何方程。只要你拿出方程，就会把大家吓跑。在今晚的某个时刻，你们所有人都会被吓到。所以大家先做好心理准备。好，咱们继续。

cues.en: There's a traditional way to start talks like this. The traditional way is to be very cultured and talk about what Democritus and Lucretius said two and a half thousand years ago and the ideas that the ancient Greeks had about atoms. But I don't want to start like this. We've made a lot of progress in two and a half thousand years and there's just better places to kick off a science talk. So the first modern picture that we had of what...
cues.zh: 通常做这类演讲有个传统的开场方式。传统的做法是显得特别有文化，大谈两千五百年前德谟克利特和卢克莱修说了什么，以及古希腊人对原子的想法。但我不想这么开场。两千五百年过去了，我们已经取得了巨大的进展，对于一场科学演讲来说，完全有更好的切入点。那么，我们对万物构成拥有的第一幅现代图景是……

cues.en: the universe is made of, everything we're made of, is this. So I hope this is familiar to most people here. This is the periodic table of elements. It's one of the most iconic images in all of science. What we have here are 120-ish different elements. I should point out, no less than 10 of which were discovered in this very building.
cues.zh: 宇宙由什么构成，我们由什么构成，就是这个。希望大家大多都认得，这是元素周期表。它是整个科学界最具标志性的图像之一。这里有大约120种不同元素。我得指出，其中至少10种就是在这栋楼里发现的。

cues.en: and which constitutes, or at least in the 1800s, were thought to constitute everything that existed in nature. So it's certainly true that any material you get, you can distill it down into its component parts, and you'll find that all of those component parts are made of one of these 120 elements. So it's a great moment in science. It's really one of the triumphs of science. It's also, I should add, the reason that I stopped doing chemistry in school.
cues.zh: 这些元素构成了，至少在19世纪人们认为构成了自然界存在的一切。所以确实，任何材料你都能分解成组成它的部分，而你会发现所有这些组成部分都由这120种元素之一构成。这是科学史上的伟大时刻，确实是科学的胜利之一。我还得说，这也是我在学校不再学化学的原因。

cues.en: Because if you're a chemist, this is basically as good as it gets. And if we're honest, it's kind of a mess.
cues.zh: 因为如果你是化学家，这基本就是天花板了。说实话，这还挺乱的。

cues.en: Everything in the universe is classified into things on the left that go bang if you put them in water through to things on the right, which really, if we're honest, don't do very much at all. You kind of organize everything into this stupid shape, so it looks a little bit like Australia. There's a big dip in the top, and then there's these two strips of elements that you have to put along the bottom because there's no room for them in the middle where they belong. I don't know about you. If I was asked to come up with a fundamental classification of everything in the universe, this isn't what I would have gone for.
cues.zh: 宇宙万物被分类，从左边放进水里会砰的一下，到右边说实话几乎不怎么反应。你把一切组织成这个蠢形状，看起来还有点像澳大利亚。顶部有个大凹陷，还有两条元素得放到底部，因为中间本该在的位置没地方。我不知道你怎样，但如果让我给宇宙万物做个基本分类，我不会选这个。

cues.en: Are there any chemists in the audience? I'm sorry for you. OK, but I'm not alone in this. It's not just me that thinks this is a silly way to organize nature. Nature itself thinks this is a silly way to organize nature. Of course, we know this isn't the fundamental... This isn't the end of the story. This isn't the fundamental building blocks. And the first person to realize that there's something deeper...
cues.zh: 观众里有化学家吗？我为你们感到遗憾。好吧，但我不是唯一这么想的人。不只是我觉得这是组织自然的蠢办法。自然界自己也觉得这是组织自然的蠢办法。当然，我们知道这不是根本……这不是故事的终点。这不是基本构建块。而第一个意识到还有更深层东西的人……

cues.en: than this, was a Cambridge physicist called J.J. Thomson. So at the end of the 1800s, J.J. Thomson discovered a particle that was smaller than an atom that we now call the electron. And in 1897, he announced this in this room, in fact, in this very lecture series,
cues.zh: 比这更深层，是剑桥物理学家 J.J. Thomson。19世纪末，J.J. Thomson 发现了一种比原子更小的粒子，我们现在叫它电子。1897年，他就在这个房间宣布了这件事，事实上就在这个讲座系列上，

cues.en: to a stunned audience. An audience that was so stunned, at least half of them didn't believe what he was saying. There was one very distinguished scientist who afterwards told J.J. Thompson he thought the whole thing was a hoax, that J.J. Thompson had just been pulling their leg. But of course, it's not a hoax. This isn't the fundamental elements of nature. And within 15 years of J.J. Thompson's discovery,
cues.zh: 面对一群震惊的听众。听众震惊到至少一半人不相信他说的话。后来有一位非常杰出的科学家告诉 J.J. Thompson，他觉得整件事是个骗局，J.J. Thompson 只是在逗他们。但当然，这不是骗局。这不是自然的基本元素。而在 J.J. Thompson 发现后的15年内，

cues.en: his successor in Cambridge, a man called Ernest Rutherford, had figured out exactly what these atoms are made of. And this is the picture that Rutherford came up with. So we now know that each of these elements consists of a nucleus, which is tiny, the metaphor that Rutherford himself used was like a fly in the center of the cathedral, and then orbiting...
cues.zh: 他在剑桥的继任者，一个叫 Ernest Rutherford 的人，弄清了原子到底由什么构成。这就是 Rutherford 提出的图景。我们现在知道，每种元素都由一个原子核构成，原子核很小，Rutherford 自己用的比喻就像大教堂中央的一只苍蝇，然后还有东西在绕着他转……

cues.en: this nucleus in, I should add, fairly blurry orbits are the electrons, which sort of fill out very sparsely the rest of the space. So that's our picture of these atoms. Subsequently, we learned that the nucleus is not itself fundamental. The nucleus contains smaller particles. They're particles that we call protons and neutrons. And in the 1970s,
cues.zh: 围绕这个原子核的，我还得补充一句，是轨道相当模糊的电子，它们稀疏地填充了其余的空间，这就是我们对这些原子的认知图景。随后我们认识到，原子核本身并非最基本的存在，原子核内部包含着更小的粒子，也就是我们所说的质子和中子。到了20世纪70年代，

cues.en: we learned that the protons and neutrons aren't fundamental either. So in the 1970s, we learned that inside each proton and neutron are three smaller particles that we call quarks. There are two different kinds of quarks. By the 1970s, I'm guessing physicists didn't have a classical Greek education, and they'd kind of run out of, you know, classy names. So we call these quarks the up quark and the down quark.
cues.zh: 我们又发现质子和中子同样不是最基本的。在20世纪70年代，我们了解到每个质子和中子内部都含有三个更小的粒子，我们称之为夸克。夸克有两种不同的类型。到了20世纪70年代，我猜物理学家们没受过古典希腊语教育，而且能用的优雅名字也用光了，所以我们把这两种夸克叫做上夸克和下夸克。

cues.en: OK? For no good reason. It's not like the up quark is higher than the down quark. It's not like it points up. And just no good reason at all. The up quark and the down quark. So the proton consists of two up quarks and a down quark. And the neutron consists of two down quarks and an up quark. OK? This, as far as we know, are the fundamental building blocks of nature. We've never discovered anything smaller than the electron. And we've never discovered anything smaller than the quarks.
cues.zh: 懂吧？根本没什么特别的原因。并不是说上夸克比下夸克位置更高，也不是说它朝上指，纯粹没有任何特别的理由，就叫上夸克和下夸克。质子由两个上夸克和一个下夸克组成，而中子由两个下夸克和一个上夸克组成，明白吧？据我们目前所知，这些就是构成自然界的最基本砌块。我们从未发现过比电子更小的东西，也从未发现过比夸克更小的东西。

cues.en: So we have three particles of which everything we know is made. And it's worth stressing. That's kind of astonishing. You know, we sort of take it for granted. We learn this in school. We don't really think about it deeply. Everything we see in the world, all the diversity in the natural world, you, me, everything around us, we're just the same three particles with slightly different rearrangements repeated over and over and over again.
cues.zh: 所以构成我们所知万物的，其实就只有这三种粒子。这一点值得着重强调，其实相当惊人。我们往往觉得这是理所当然的，在学校里学过，却从未真正深思过：世间所见的一切、自然界的种种多样性、你、我、我们周围的万事万物，不过都是这三种相同的粒子，以稍微不同的排列方式反反复复地重组而成的。

cues.en: It's an amazing lesson to draw about how the world is put together. So that's what we have. We have an electron and two quarks. And these aren't the fundamental building blocks that the Greeks had thought about, and they're certainly not the fundamental building blocks that the Victorians had thought about. But the spirit of the issue really hasn't changed. The spirit is exactly what democracies said
cues.zh: 对于世界是如何构成的，这是一个令人惊叹的启示。所以我们拥有的就是：一个电子和两种夸克。这些固然不是古希腊人所设想的基本砌块，也肯定不是维多利亚时代人所想的那样，但这个问题的精神实质其实从未改变。这种精神实质完全符合德谟克利特

cues.en: 2,500 years ago, it's that there are like Lego bricks from which everything in the world is constructed. These Lego bricks are particles, and the particles are the electron and two quarks. It's a very nice picture. It's a very comforting picture. It's the picture we teach kids at school. It's the picture we even teach our students in undergraduate university. And there's a problem with it. The problem is, it's a lie.
cues.zh: 在2500年前的说法：世界万物就像是用乐高积木搭建起来的。这些乐高积木就是粒子，也就是电子和两种夸克。这幅图景非常美好，也非常让人安心，是我们在学校教给孩子的图景，甚至也是我们在大学本科教给学生的图景。然而它有一个问题：问题在于，它其实是个谎言。

cues.en: It's a white lie. It's a white lie that we tell our children because we don't want to expose them to the difficult and horrible truth too early on. It makes it easier to learn if you believe that these particles are the fundamental building blocks of the universe. But it's simply not true. The best theories that we have of physics do not have underlying them the quark particle and the two quark particles. Sorry, the electron particle and the two quark particles.
cues.zh: 这是一个善意的谎言。这是我们告诉孩子的善意谎言，因为不想让他们过早接触艰难又可怕的真相。如果你相信这些粒子是宇宙的基本构件，学起来会更容易。但事实并非如此。我们最好的物理学理论，底层并不是夸克粒子和两种夸克粒子。抱歉，是电子粒子和两种夸克粒子。

cues.en: In fact, the very best theories we have of physics don't rely on particles at all. The best theories we have tell us that the fundamental building blocks of nature are not particles, but something much more nebulous and abstract. The fundamental building blocks of nature are fluid-like substances which are spread throughout the entire universe and ripple in strange and interesting ways.
cues.zh: 事实上，我们拥有的最顶尖物理学理论根本不依赖粒子。我们最好的理论告诉我们，自然界的基本构件不是粒子，而是某种更加模糊、抽象的东西。自然界的基本构件是类流体物质，它们遍布整个宇宙，并以奇特而有趣的方式起伏波动。

cues.en: OK? That's the fundamental reality in which we live. These fluid-like substances we have a name for, we call them fields. So this is a picture of a field. This isn't the kind of field that physicists have in mind. This is what you think a field is if you're a farmer or if you're a normal person. If you're a physicist, you have a very different picture in your mind when you think about fields. And I'll tell you the ...
cues.zh: 好吗？这就是我们所处的基本现实。这些类流体物质有名字，我们叫它们场。所以这是一张场的图。这不是物理学家心中的那种场。如果你是农民或普通人，你会以为场就是这样。如果你是物理学家，想到场时，脑海中会有非常不同的图景。我会告诉你们这个……

cues.en: the general definition of a field, and then we'll go through some examples so that you get familiar with this. The physicist's definition of a field is the following. It's something that, as I said, is spread everywhere throughout the universe. It's something that takes a particular value at every point in space, and what's more, that value can change in time. So the picture to have in your mind is a fluid, which ripples and sways throughout the universe.
cues.zh: 场的通用定义，然后我们会讲几个例子，好让你熟悉它。物理学家对场的定义是这样的。它是某种如我所说遍布整个宇宙的东西。它是某种在空间每一点取特定值的东西，而且这个值还能随时间变化。所以要在脑海中构想的图景是一种流体，它在整个宇宙中泛起涟漪、来回摆动。

cues.en: Now, it's not a new idea. It's not an idea that we've just come up with. It's an idea which dates back almost 200 years, and like so many other things in science, it's an idea which originated in this very room. Because, as I'm sure many of you are aware, this is the home of Michael Faraday.
cues.zh: 现在，这不是一个新想法。这不是我们刚刚想出来的想法。这个想法可以追溯到近200年前，而且和科学中许多其他东西一样，它起源于这个房间。因为我相信你们很多人都知道，这里是Michael Faraday的家。

cues.en: And Michael Faraday initiated this lecture series in 1825. He gave over 100 of these Friday evening discourses, and the vast majority of these were on his own discoveries on the experiments he did on electricity and magnetism. So he did many, many things in electricity and magnetism over many decades, and in doing so, he built up an intuition for how electric and magnetic phenomena
cues.zh: Michael Faraday在1825年创办了这个系列讲座。他做了100多场这样的周五晚间演讲，其中绝大多数都关于他自己的发现，也就是他在电和磁方面所做的实验。所以几十年来，他在电和磁方面做了很多很多事情，也由此建立起对电磁现象如何

cues.en: work, and the intuition is what we now call the electric and magnetic field. So what he envisaged was that, threaded everywhere throughout space, were these invisible objects called the electric and magnetic fields. Now, we learn this in school. Again, it's something that we sort of take for granted, because we learn it at an early age, and we don't...
cues.zh: 运作的直觉，也就是我们现在所说的电场和磁场。所以他设想的是，这些被称为电场和磁场的不可见物体，贯穿整个空间。现在，我们在学校里学到这个。再说一次，这是我们有点习以为常的东西，因为我们很小就学了，而且我们不……

cues.en: sort of appreciate just how big of a radical step this idea of Faraday's is. I want to stress, it's one of the most revolutionary abstract ideas in the history of science, that these electric and magnetic fields exist. So let me just ... You're supposed to do demonstrations in this, and I'm not just a theoretical physicist, I'm a very theoretical physicist. It's very hard for me to do any kind of experiment that's going to work, but I'm just going to show you something that you've all seen.
cues.zh: 或多或少能体会到法拉第的这一想法有多么激进。我想强调的是，电场和磁场的存在，是科学史上最具颠覆性的抽象思想之一。所以让我来……按说我该在这儿做些演示，但我不仅是个理论物理学家，还是个极其纯粹的理论物理学家。对我来说，做任何能成功的实验都太难了，但我还是要给你们看一样大家都见过的东西。

cues.en: They're magnets, okay? And we all played these games when we were kids or when we were in school. You take these magnets and you move them together, and as they get closer and closer, there's this force that you can sort of just feel building up that pushes the pressure, that pushes against these two magnets. And it doesn't matter how often you do it, and it doesn't matter how many degrees you have in physics, it's just a little bit magical.
cues.zh: 这是磁铁，对吧？我们小时候或上学时都玩过这个游戏。拿两块磁铁互相靠近，越靠越近时，你能隐约感觉到一股力在逐渐增强，推挤着这两块磁铁。不管你试过多少次，也不管你拿了多少物理学学位，这种感觉总有那么一点神奇。

cues.en: You know, you all know this. There's something just special about this weird feeling that you get between magnets. And this was Faraday's genius. It was to appreciate that even though you can't see anything in between, even though no matter how closely you look, the space between these magnets will seem to be empty, he said, nonetheless, there's something real there. There's something real and physical which is invisible but is building up.
cues.zh: 你们懂的，大家都知道这种感觉。磁铁之间的这种奇妙感受确实非同寻常。而这就是法拉第的天才之处。他敏锐地意识到，尽管中间什么都看不见，尽管无论你凑多近看，磁铁之间的空间似乎都是空无一物，但他坚信，那里确实存在着某种真实的东西。存在着某种看不见却在不断积聚的、真实而有形的东西。

cues.en: and that's what's responsible for the force. So he called them lines of force. We now call it the magnetic field. So this, of course, is a picture of Michael Faraday. This is a picture of Michael Faraday lecturing behind this very table. Here is a drawing from one of Michael Faraday's papers. It was pointed out to me earlier. When you leave, there's a carpet just here. The carpet has this pattern. This picture just repeated on it over and over and over again.
cues.zh: 而这正是那股力的来源。于是他将其称作“力线”。也就是我们现在所说的磁场。当然，这就是 Michael Faraday 的画像。这是 Michael Faraday 就在这张讲台后演讲的画作。这张是出自 Michael Faraday 一篇论文的手绘图。刚才有人提醒我，大家离开时，会看到这边有一块地毯，地毯上的图案就是这幅图在一遍又一遍地重复。

cues.en: And on the bottom here is one of Michael Faraday's most famous demonstrations that he did here. So I'll just walk you through what Faraday did. The thing on the right, there's a small coil with a hand on it. This is a battery, and the battery passes a current around this coil, and in doing so, there's a magnetic field that's induced in this. It's what's called a solenoid.
cues.zh: 下面这个是 Michael Faraday 当年在此处所做的最著名的演示之一。我来带大家看一下法拉第做了什么。右边这个，是一个上面有只手的小线圈。这是一个电池，电池让电流绕着这个线圈流动，这样一来，里面就感应出了磁场。这就是所谓的螺线管。

cues.en: And then Faraday did the following thing. He simply moved this small coil, A, through this big coil, B, like this. And something miraculous happened. When you do that, there's a moving magnetic field. Faraday's great discovery was induction. It gives rise to a current in B, which then, over on this end of the table, makes a needle flicker like this. So extremely simple.
cues.zh: 接着法拉第做了这么一件事。他只是把这个小线圈 A，像这样穿过这个大线圈 B。奇迹发生了。当你这么做时，就产生了一个运动的磁场。法拉第的伟大发现就是电磁感应。它在 B 中激发了电流，随后在桌子的这一头，让指针像这样摆动了起来。就是这么极其简单。

cues.en: You move a magnetic field, and it gives rise to a current, which makes a needle flicker on the other side of the table. This astounded audience is in the 1800s. Because you were doing something and affecting the needle on the other end of the table, yet you never touched the needle. It was amazing. You could make something move without ever going near it, without ever touching it.
cues.zh: 你移动磁场，就会产生电流，让桌子另一端的指针颤动。这让19世纪的观众大为震惊。因为你在做某件事，影响了桌子另一端的指针，却从没碰过那根指针。太神奇了。你能让某个东西动起来，却从不靠近它，从不触碰它。

cues.en: We kind of jaded these days. You can do the same experiment. You can pick out your cellphone, you can press a few buttons, you can call somebody on the other end of the Earth within seconds. But it's the same principle, but this was the first time it was demonstrated that the field is real. You can communicate using the field. You can affect things far away using the field without ever touching it. So this is Michael Faraday's legacy. It's that there's not just particles in the world, there's other objects that are slightly more subtle
cues.zh: 如今我们有点见怪不怪了。你可以做同样的实验。掏出手机，按几个按钮，几秒内就能打给地球另一端的人。原理是一样的，但这是第一次证明场是真实存在的。你可以用场来通信。你可以用场影响远处的东西，却从不接触它。所以这是 Michael Faraday 的遗产。也就是说，世界上不只有粒子，还有其他一些更微妙的实体

cues.en: that are called fields that are spread throughout all of space. By the way, if you ever want to really appreciate the genius of Michael Faraday, he gave this lecture in 1846. He gave many lectures in 1846, but there was one in particular where he finished 20 minutes early. He ran out of things to say. So he engaged in some idle speculation for 20 minutes. And Faraday suggested...
cues.zh: 它们叫作场，遍布整个空间。顺便说，如果你想真正领略 Michael Faraday 的天才，他1846年做过这场演讲。1846年他讲过很多场，但特别有一场，他提前20分钟结束了。他没东西可讲了。于是他就即兴空想了20分钟。然后 Faraday 提出……

cues.en: that these invisible electric and magnetic fields that had postulated were quite literally the only thing we've ever seen. He suggested that it's ripples of the electric and magnetic field, which is what we call light. So it took, of course, 50 years for people like Maxwell and Hertz to confirm that this is indeed what light is made of, but it was Faraday's genius that appreciated this, that there are waves in the electric magnetic field, and those waves are the light
cues.zh: 这些不可见的电场和磁场——他假设存在的——字面意义上就是我们所见的一切。他提出，电磁场的涟漪就是我们所说的光。当然，50年后 Maxwell 和 Hertz 等人才证实光确实由它构成；但正是 Faraday 的天才洞见到了这一点：电磁场中存在波，而那些波就是光

cues.en: we see around us. Okay, so this is Faraday's legacy. But it turns out this idea of fields was much more important than Faraday had realized. And it took over 150 years for us to appreciate the importance of these fields. So what happened in these 150 years was that there was a small revolution in science. In the 1920s, we realized that the world is very, very different from
cues.zh: 也就是我们周围看到的光。好，这就是 Faraday 的遗产。但事实证明，场的概念远比 Faraday 意识到的更重要。我们花了150多年才认识到这些场的重要性。这150年里发生了一场科学上的小革命。20世纪20年代，我们意识到世界与……非常非常不同

cues.en: the common sense ideas that Newton and Galileo had handed down to us centuries before. So in the 1920s, people like Heisenberg and Schrödinger realized that on the smallest scales, on the microscopic scales, the world is much more mysterious and counterintuitive than we ever really imagined it could be. This, of course, is the theory that we now know as quantum mechanics.
cues.zh: 几个世纪前 Newton 和 Galileo 传给我们的常识观念。所以在20世纪20年代，Heisenberg 和 Schrödinger 这样的人意识到，在最小尺度上、在微观尺度上，世界比我们真正想象过的要神秘得多、反直觉得多。当然，这就是我们现在所说的量子力学。

cues.en: So there's a lot I could say about quantum mechanics. Let me tell you one of the punch lines of quantum mechanics. One of the punch lines is that energy isn't continuous. Energy in the world is always parceled up into some little discreet lump. That's actually what the word quantum means. Quantum means discreet or lumpy.
cues.zh: 关于量子力学，我可以说的有很多。我先告诉大家量子力学的核心结论之一。其中一个核心结论就是：能量不是连续的。世间的所有能量，总是被打包成一小块一小块离散的团块。这其实就是“量子”这个词的含义。量子，指的就是离散的、成团的。

cues.en: The real fun starts when you try and take the ideas of quantum mechanics, which say that things should be discrete, and you try to combine them with Faraday's ideas of fields, which are very much continuous, smooth objects which are waving and oscillating in space. So the idea of trying to combine these two theories together is what we call quantum field theory.
cues.zh: 真正有意思的地方在于，当你试图把量子力学中“事物应当是离散的”这一思想，与法拉第的“场”理论结合起来时——而场是非常连续、平滑，且在空间中波动和振荡的实体。把这两种理论融合在一起的想法，就是我们所说的量子场论。

cues.en: And here's the implication of quantum field theory. The first implication is what happens for the electric and magnetic field. So Faraday taught us, and Maxwell later, that waves of the electromagnetic field are what we call light. But when you apply quantum mechanics to this, you find that these light waves aren't quite as smooth and continuous as they appeared. So if you look closely at light waves, you'll find that they're made of particles.
cues.zh: 这就是量子场论带来的推论。第一个推论是关于电场和磁场的。法拉第以及后来的麦克斯韦告诉我们，电磁场的波动就是我们所说的光。但当你把量子力学应用到这里时，你会发现这些光波并不像表面上看起来那么平滑和连续。如果你仔细观察光波，就会发现它们是由粒子构成的。

cues.en: They're little particles of light, and these are particles that we call the photon. The magic of this idea is that that same principle applies to every single other particle in the universe. So there is, spread everywhere throughout this room, something that we call the electron field. It's like a fluid that fills this room and in fact fills the entire universe.
cues.zh: 它们是光的微小粒子，这些粒子就是我们所说的光子。这种思想的奇妙之处在于，同样的原理适用于宇宙中的每一种其他粒子。在这个房间里，到处弥漫着一种我们称之为电子场的东西。它就像一种流体，充满了这个房间，实际上也充满了整个宇宙。

cues.en: And the ripples of this electron fluid, the waves of this fluid, get tied into little bundles of energy by the rules of quantum mechanics, and those bundles of energy are what we call the particle, the electron. All the electrons that are in your body are not fundamental. All the electrons that exist in your body are waves of the same underlying field. We're all connected to each other.
cues.zh: 根据量子力学的规律，这种电子流体的涟漪、这种流体的波动，会被束缚成一个个微小的能量包，而这些能量包就是我们所说的粒子——电子。你体内的所有电子都不是最根本的基础。你体内存在的所有电子，都是同一个底层场的波动。我们彼此之间都是相连的。

cues.en: The waves on the ocean all belong to the same underlying ocean. The electrons in your body are the ripples of the same field as the electrons in my body. There's more than this. There's also, in this room, two quark fields. And the ripples of these two quark fields give rise to what we call the up quark and the down quark. And the same is true for every other kind of particle in the universe. There are fields that underlie everything.
cues.zh: 海洋上的波浪都属于同一片底层的大海。你体内的电子，和我体内的电子，都是同一个场的涟漪。不仅如此，在这个房间里，还存在着两种夸克场。这两种夸克场的涟漪，孕育出了我们所说的上夸克和下夸克。宇宙中的其他所有粒子也都是如此。场，是一切事物的基础。

cues.en: And what we think of as particles aren't really particles at all, they're waves of these fields, tied up into little bundles of energy. So this is the legacy of Faraday. This is where Faraday's vision of fields has taken us. There are no particles in the world. The basic fundamental building blocks of our universe are these fluid-like substances that we call fields. All right. OK.
cues.zh: 而我们所认为的粒子，其实根本不是粒子，它们是这些场的波动，被捆绑成了一个个微小的能量包。这就是法拉第留下的遗产。这就是法拉第对“场”的远见带给我们的认识。世界上根本没有粒子。我们宇宙最基本的基石，其实是这些类似流体的实体，我们称之为“场”。好了。

cues.en: So what I want to do in the rest of this talk is tell you where that vision takes us. I want to tell you about what it means that we're not made of particles. We're made of fields. And I want to tell you what we can do with that and how we can best understand the universe around us. So here's the first thing. Take a box.
cues.zh: 在接下来的演讲里，我想告诉大家这个图景会把我们带向哪里。我想谈谈我们不是由粒子构成的，而是由场构成的，这意味着什么。我还想告诉大家，我们能拿它做什么，以及怎样才能最好地理解周围的宇宙。先说第一件事：拿一个盒子。

cues.en: and take every single thing that exists out of that box. Take all the particles out of the box, all the atoms out of the box. What you're left with is a pure vacuum, and this is what the vacuum looks like. So what you're looking at here is a computer simulation using our best theory of physics. It's something called the Standard Model, which I'll introduce later. But it's a computer simulation of absolutely nothing. This is empty.
cues.zh: 把盒子里存在的每一样东西都拿出来。把所有粒子都拿出来，把所有原子都拿出来。剩下的是纯真空，而真空就是这个样子。你现在看到的是用我们最好的物理理论做的计算机模拟。这个理论叫标准模型，我后面会介绍。但它模拟的是彻彻底底的“什么都没有”。这里是空的。

cues.en: space, literally empty space with nothing in it. This is the simplest thing you could possibly imagine in the universe. And you can see it's an interesting place to be, empty space. It's not dull and boring. What you're looking at here is that even when the particles are taken out, the field still exists. The field is there. But what's more, the field is governed by the rules of quantum mechanics.
cues.zh: 空间，字面意义上空无一物的空间。这是你能在宇宙中想象到的最简单的东西。你能看到，空无一物的空间其实是个很有意思的地方。它并不枯燥无聊。你在这里看到的是：即使粒子都被拿走了，场仍然存在。场就在那里。更重要的是，场受量子力学规律支配。

cues.en: And there's a principle in quantum mechanics, which is called the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, which says you're not allowed to sit still, and the field has to obey this. So even when there's nothing else there, the field is constantly bubbling and fluctuating in what's quite honestly a very complicated way. These are things that we call quantum vacuum fluctuations. But this is what nothingness looks like from the perspective of our current theories of physics.
cues.zh: 量子力学里有一个原理，叫海森堡不确定性原理，它说你不允许静止不动，场也必须遵守这一点。所以即使那里没有别的东西，场也在不断翻涌、涨落，老实说，方式非常复杂。我们把这些东西称为量子真空涨落。但在我们当前物理理论的视角下，这就是“虚无”的样子。

cues.en: It's worth saying that this is a computer simulation. It looks a little bit like a cartoon, but it's actually quite a powerful computer simulation that it took a long time to do. But these aren't just theoretical. These quantum fluctuations that are there in the pure vacuum are things that we can measure. There's something called the Casimir force. The Casimir force is a force between two metal plates that get pushed together basically because there's more of this stuff on the outside than on the inside.
cues.zh: 值得一提的是，这是一个计算机模拟。它看起来有点像卡通，但它其实是很强大的计算机模拟，花了很长时间才做出来。但这些不只是理论。纯真空中存在的这些量子涨落，是我们能够测量的东西。有一种东西叫卡西米尔力。卡西米尔力是两块金属板之间的力，它们会被推到一起，基本上是因为外侧的这种东西比内侧多。

cues.en: And these are real. These are things that we can measure, and they behave just as we would predict they would from our theories. So this is nothing. And this brings me to the more mathematical side of the talk, because there's a challenge in this. This is the simplest thing we can imagine in the entire universe, and it's complicated.
cues.zh: 而这些都是真的。这些是我们能测量的东西，它们的行为正好符合我们理论的预测。所以，这就是“虚无”。这也把我带到演讲中更数学的一面，因为这里有个挑战。这是我们在整个宇宙中能想象到的最简单的东西，可它却很复杂。

cues.en: OK, it's astonishingly complicated. And it doesn't get easier than this. You know, if you want to now understand not nothing but a single particle, well, that's much more complicated than this. And if you want to understand 10 to the 23 particles all doing something interesting, that's really, really much more complicated than this. So there's a problem in, well, it's my problem, not yours, in addressing this fundamental description of the universe, which is that it's just hard.
cues.zh: 好吧，它复杂得惊人。而且这已经是最简单的情况了。你知道，如果你现在想理解的不是“虚无”，而是单个粒子，那可比这复杂得多。如果你想理解 10 的 23 次方个粒子一起做出有趣的事情，那就真的、真的要复杂得多。所以，在给出这种对宇宙的基础描述时有个问题——好吧，这是我的问题，不是你的问题——那就是：它真的很难。

cues.en: The mathematics that we use to describe quantum fields, to describe everything that we're made of in terms of quantum fields, is substantially more difficult than the maths that arises in any other area of physics or science. It's genuinely difficult. I can put this in some perspective. There's a list of six...
cues.zh: 我们用来描述量子场、用量子场来描述构成我们万物的数学，要比物理学或科学中任何其他领域的数学都难得多。是真的非常难。我可以换个角度来解释。有一份包含六个……

cues.en: open problems in mathematics. They're considered to be the six hardest problems in mathematics. There used to be seven, but some crazy Russian guy solved one of them. So there's six left. You win a million bucks if you can solve any one of these problems. If you know a little bit of mathematics, they're things like the Riemann hypothesis, or P versus NP, and they're sort of famously difficult problems. This is one of those six problems. You win a million dollars if you can understand this.
cues.zh: 数学未解难题的清单。它们被公认为数学界最难的六道题目。原本有七道，但一个疯狂的俄罗斯老哥解出了其中一道。所以现在还剩六道。只要解出其中任何一道，你就能赢得一百万美元。如果你懂一点数学，就会知道像黎曼猜想、P 与 NP 问题这类赫赫有名的难题。而眼前这个就是那六大难题之一。如果你能彻底搞懂它，就能拿下一百万美元。

cues.en: So what does it mean? It doesn't mean can you build a big computer and just demonstrate that these are there. It means can you understand from first principles by solving the equations the patterns that emerge within these quantum fluctuations? It's an extraordinarily difficult problem. It's right in the kind of thing I do. I don't know a single person in the world who's actually working on this problem. That's how hard it is. We don't really even know how to begin to start understanding
cues.zh: 那这到底是什么意思呢？并不是说你能造一台超级计算机把它们演示出来就行。而是说，你能不能从第一性原理出发，通过解方程来理解这些量子涨落中涌现出来的模式？这是一个难到不可思议的问题。这恰好属于我的研究范畴。但全世界我找不出一个人目前正在攻克这个问题。它就是这么难。我们甚至根本不知道该从何入手去理解

cues.en: these kind of ideas in quantum field theory. Okay. This theme about the mathematics being challenging is something which is going to come back later in the talk. So I'd like just to take a little bit of a diversion for a few minutes and give you a sense about what we can do mathematically and what we can't do mathematically. Just sort of tell you what the state of play is in terms of a...
cues.zh: 量子场论中的这类思想。好。关于数学极具挑战性这个话题，稍后的演讲中我们还会谈到。所以接下来我想先稍微岔开几分钟，让大家感受一下我们在数学上能做到什么，以及做不到什么。也就是大概讲讲目前的现状……

cues.en: us understanding these theories, called quantum field theories, which underlie our universe. So there are times where we understand extremely well what's going on with quantum fields. And that happens basically when these fluctuations are very calm and tame, when they're not wild and strong. These ones are big, but when they're much more calmer, when the vacuum is much more like a mill pond than it is like a ...
cues.zh: 关于我们对这些构筑了宇宙基石的“量子场论”的理解程度。有些时候，我们对量子场中发生的事情理解得非常透彻。基本上就是在这些涨落非常平静、温和，而不是狂暴、剧烈的时候。眼前的这些涨落很大，但如果它们平静得多，当真空更像一池静水而不是……

cues.en: a raging storm. In those cases, we really think we understand what we're doing. And to illustrate this, I just want to give you this example. So this number G is a particular property of the electron particle. And I'll quickly explain what it is. The electron is a particle, and it turns out the electron spins. It orbits rather like the Earth.
cues.zh: 狂暴的风暴时，在那种情况下，我们确实认为自己完全搞懂了。为了说明这一点，我想给大家看这个例子。这个数值 g 是电子的一种特殊性质。我快速解释一下它是什么。电子是一种粒子，事实证明电子会自旋。它的自转很像地球

cues.en: orbits. And it has an axis of spin, and you can change the axis of that spin. And the way you change it is you take a magnetic field like this, and in the presence of a magnetic field, the electron will spin, the electron will stay in one place but spin, and then the axis of spin will slowly rotate like this. It's what's called precession. And the speed at which the axis of that spin processes is dictated by this number here.
cues.zh: 自转。它有一个自旋轴，而且你可以改变这个自旋轴的方向。改变的方法是施加这样一个磁场，在磁场存在的情况下，电子会自旋，电子会停留在原地并自旋，然后它的自旋轴会像这样慢慢转动。这就是所谓的进动。而这个自旋轴进动的速度，就是由这里的这个数值决定的。

cues.en: So it's not the most important thing in the big picture. However, historically, this has been extremely important in the history of physics because it turns out this is a number you can measure very, very accurately doing experiments. And so this number has sort of acted as a testing ground for us to see how well we understand the theories that underline nature and in particular quantum field theory. So let me tell you what you're looking at here. The first number
cues.zh: 从大局来看，它并不是最重要的。然而，从历史上看，它在物理学史上却极其重要，因为事实证明，你可以通过实验非常非常精确地测出这个数值。所以这个数值就成了一个试验场，用来检验我们对自然界底层理论——尤其是量子场论——的理解程度。接下来我给大家解释一下眼前看到的这些内容。第一个数值

cues.en: is the result of many, many decades of painstaking experiments measuring very, very precisely this feature of the electron. It's called the magnetic moment. And the second number is the result of many, many decades of very tortuous calculations sitting down with a pen and paper and trying to predict from first principles, from quantum field theory,
cues.zh: 是数十年来极其艰苦的实验结果，极为精确地测量了电子的这一特性，它被称为磁矩。而第二个数字则是数十年来极为艰难的理论推演成果，人们伏案执笔，试图依据第一性原理、从量子场论出发进行预测，

cues.en: what the magnetic moment of the electron should be. And you can see, it's simply spectacular. There's nothing like this anywhere else in science with an agreement between the theoretical calculation and the experimental measurements. I think it's 12 or 13 significant figures. It's really astonishing. Any other area of science, you'll be jumping up and down for joy if you get the first two numbers right. Economics, not even that.
cues.zh: 电子的磁矩应该是多少。你可以看到，这简直令人叹为观止。在整个科学界，理论计算与实验测量之间，绝无如此高度一致的先例。我想这精确到了 12 或 13 位有效数字。真的太惊人了。在科学的其他任何领域，只要前两位数字能对上，你都会高兴得手舞足蹈。而经济学呢，连这都做不到。

cues.en: But this is where we're at in particle physics. On a good day, when we really understand what we're doing, it's substantially better than any other area of science. Twelve significant figures. But this, of course, I've shown you, because this is our best result. There are many other results that are nowhere near as good. And the difficulty comes when those quantum vacuum fluctuations start getting wilder and stronger. So let me give you an example. It should be possible for us
cues.zh: 但这就是粒子物理学目前的现状。状态好的时候，当我们真正搞懂自己在做什么时，它的表现远好于任何其他科学领域。能达到十二位有效数字。当然，我给你们看这个，是因为这是我们最棒的成果。还有很多其他结果，远远没有这么理想。而困难就在于，当那些量子真空涨落开始变得越来越剧烈、越来越强时。让我给你们举个例子。按理说我们应该能够

cues.en: to sit down and calculate from first principles the mass of the proton. We have the equations, everything should be there, we just need to work hard and figure out what the mass of the proton is just by doing calculations. We've been trying to do this for about 40 years now. We can get it to within an accuracy of something like 3 percent.
cues.zh: 坐下来从第一性原理计算出质子的质量。方程我们都有，一切理应都在那里，我们只需要下功夫，光靠计算就能得出质子的质量。这件事情我们已经尝试了大约 40 年。目前我们能算出的精度大概在 3% 以内。

cues.en: Which isn't bad. We're 3% there, but we should be much, much better. We should be sort of pushing these levels of accuracy. And the reason is it's very simple. We've got the right equation. We're pretty sure we're solving the right equation. It's simply that we're not smart enough to solve it. 40 years, the world's most powerful computers, lots and lots of smart people, but we haven't managed to figure this out yet.
cues.zh: 这还算不错，我们完成了3%，但我们本该做得好得多。我们本该去冲击这样的精度水平。原因其实非常简单。我们掌握了正确的方程式。我们非常确信自己解的是对的方程。仅仅是因为我们还不够聪明，解不出它来。整整40年，世界上最强大的计算机，无数聪明绝顶的人，但我们至今都还没能把它彻底搞明白。

cues.en: OK. There are other situations that I won't tell you about where we don't even get off the ground. There are some situations where, for fairly subtle reasons, we're unable to use computers to help us, and we simply have no idea what we're doing. So it's a slightly strange situation. We have these theories of physics. They're the best theories we've ever developed, as you can see by this. But at the same time, they're also the theories that we understand the least.
cues.zh: 好。还有一些情况我不会讲，那些情况我们根本没法起步。有些情况出于相当微妙的原因，我们无法借助计算机，而且我们根本不知道自己在做什么。所以情况有点奇怪。我们有这些物理理论。它们是我们开发过的最好的理论，你从这就能看出来。但与此同时，它们也是我们理解得最少的理论。

cues.en: To make progress, we sort of have this strange balancing act between increasing our theoretical understanding and figuring out how to apply that to the experiments that we're doing. And again, it's a theme I'll come back to at the end of this lecture. All right, so so far I've been talking in a little bit of generality about what we're made of. And this is the punchline for the halfway point of the talk. You're all made of quantum fields, and I don't understand them.
cues.zh: 为了取得进展，我们有点像在走钢丝：一边要加深理论理解，一边要弄清如何将其应用于我们正在做的实验。同样，这也是我在这场演讲结尾还会探讨的主题。好了，目前为止我都是很宽泛地在讲我们是由什么构成的。而这也是演讲半程的核心结论：你们都是由量子场构成的，而我并不懂它们。

cues.en: At least I don't understand them as well as I think I should. So what I want to do now is go into a little bit more specifics. I want to tell you exactly what quantum fields you're all made of. In fact, I'll tell you exactly what quantum fields exist in the universe. And the good news is that not many of them. So I'll simply tell you all of them. So we started with the periodic table. This is the new periodic table. And it's much simpler. It's much nicer.
cues.zh: 至少我自认为没能完全理解它们。所以我现在想更具体地聊一聊。我想准确告诉大家，构成你们每个人的到底是什么量子场。实际上，我要告诉你全宇宙到底存在哪些量子场。好消息是，并不多。所以我会把它们全讲出来。我们是从元素周期表开始的。而这是新的元素周期表。它更简单，也更优美。

cues.en: There are the three particles that we're all made of. There's the electron and the two quarks, the up quark and the down quark. And as I've stressed, the particles aren't fundamental. What's really fundamental is the field that underlies them. And then it turns out there's a fourth particle.
cues.zh: 构成我们所有人的就是这三种粒子。电子，以及两种夸克：上夸克和下夸克。而且正如我一直强调的，粒子并不是基本的。真正基本的，是它们底层的场。事实证明，还有第四种粒子。

cues.en: that I've not discussed so far. It's called the neutrino. It's not important in what we're made of, but it does play another important role elsewhere in the universe. These neutrinos are everywhere. You've never noticed them, but since I began this talk, something like 10 to the 14 of them have streamed through the body of each and every one of you, as many coming from above, from outer space, as actually coming from below, because they stream all the way through the Earth and then keep going.
cues.zh: 我目前还没提过它。它叫中微子。它对构成我们身体并不重要，但在宇宙的其他地方扮演着极其重要的角色。这些中微子无处不在。你从未注意到它们，但从我开讲到现在，大约有 10 的 14 次方个中微子已经穿透了你们每个人的身体；从天而降、来自外太空的数量，跟从地下穿上来的数量几乎一样多，因为它们会直接穿透整个地球，然后继续前行。

cues.en: Not very sociable, they don't interact. So this is what everything is made of. These are the four particles that form the bedrock of our universe, except then something rather strange happened. For a reason that we do not understand at all, nature has chosen to take these four particles and reproduce them twice over. So this...
cues.zh: 它们很不合群，基本不与外界相互作用。所以，这就是万物的构成。正是这四种粒子构成了我们宇宙的基石，然而紧接着一件怪事发生了。出于我们完全无法理解的原因，大自然决定把这四种粒子完完整整地复制了两次。所以，这个……

cues.en: is actually the list of all the fields that make up particles in our universe. So what are we looking at here? This is the electron. It turns out there are two other particles which behave in every way exactly the same as the electron, except they're heavier. We call them the muon, which has a mass of something like 200 times the electron, and the tau particle, which is 3,000 times heavier than the electron. Why are they there? They have no idea at all. It's one of the mysteries of the universe.
cues.zh: 实际上就是构成我们宇宙中所有粒子的场的全貌。那我们眼前看到的究竟是什么？这是电子。事实证明，还有另外两种粒子在各方面的表现都与电子一模一样，只是它们更重。我们称之为缪子——其质量大约是电子的 200 倍；以及陶子——比电子重 3000 倍。它们为什么存在？大家完全摸不着头脑。这是宇宙的未解之谜之一。

cues.en: There's also two more neutrinos. So there are three neutrinos in total. And the two quarks that we first knew about are now joined by four others that we call the strange quark and the charmed quark. And then by the time we got here, we really ran out of any kind of inspiration for naming them. We call them the bottom quark and the top quark.
cues.zh: 还有另外两种中微子。所以总共有三种中微子。我们最早知道的那两种夸克，现在又多了四种：奇异夸克、粲夸克。等走到这一步，我们实在想不出什么命名灵感了，就叫它们底夸克和顶夸克。

cues.en: So I should stress, we understand things very, very well going this way. We understand why they come in a group of four. We understand why they have the properties that they do. We don't understand it at all going this way. We don't know why there's three of these rather than two of them or 17 of them. That's a mystery. But this is everything. This is everything in the universe. Everything you're made of is...
cues.zh: 我得强调，沿着这个方向，我们理解得非常非常透彻。我们明白它们为什么成组出现四个，明白它们为什么具有这些性质。但反过来，我们完全不懂。我们不知道为什么是三个，而不是两个或十七个。这是个谜。但这就是一切。这是宇宙中的一切。构成你的一切就是……

cues.en: these three at the top there, and it's only when you go to more exotic situations, like particle colliders, that we need the others on the bottom. But every single thing we've ever seen can be made out of these 12 particles, 12 fields. These 12 fields interact with each other, and they interact through four different forces. Two of these are extremely familiar, the force of gravity and the force of electromagnetism, but there's also two other forces which operate only on small scales of a nucleus.
cues.zh: 最上面这三个，只有进入更极端的情形，比如粒子对撞机，才需要下面那些。但我们见过的每一个东西，都能由这12种粒子、12种场构成。这12种场彼此相互作用，并通过四种不同的力发生作用。其中两种我们极其熟悉：引力和电磁力；但还有另外两种力，只在原子核这样的小尺度上起作用。

cues.en: So there's something called the strong nuclear force, which holds the quarks together inside protons and neutrons, and there's something called the weak nuclear force, which is responsible for radioactive decay and, among other things, for making the sun shine. Again, each of these forces is associated to a field. So Faraday taught us about the electromagnetic field, but there's a field associated to this, which is called the gluon field, and a field associated to this, which is called the W and Z boson field. There's also...
cues.zh: 有一种叫强核力，把夸克束缚在质子和中子内部；还有一种叫弱核力，负责放射性衰变，也负责让太阳发光等等。同样，每种力都对应一种场。法拉第让我们认识了电磁场，但这里还有一种对应的场，叫胶子场；这里也有一种对应的场，叫W和Z玻色子场。还有……

cues.en: a field associated to gravity. And this was really Einstein's great insight into the world. The field associated to gravity turns out to be space and time itself. So if you've never heard that before, that was the world's shortest introduction to general relativity. And I'm not going to say anything else about it. I'll just let you figure that one out for yourself.
cues.zh: 还有一种与引力相关的场。这正是爱因斯坦对世界的伟大洞见。与引力对应的场，原来就是空间和时间本身。如果你以前没听过，这就是世界上最短的广义相对论入门。这个我就不多说了，留给你自己琢磨。

cues.en: This is the universe we live in. There are 12 fields that give matter, I'll call them matter fields, and four other fields that are the forces. And the world we live in is these combination of the 16 fields, all interacting together in interesting ways. So this is what you should think of the universe as like. It's filled with these fields, fluid-like substances. 12 matter, 4 forces.
cues.zh: 这就是我们生活的宇宙。有12种场构成物质，我叫它们物质场；还有4种场对应力。我们生活的世界，就是这16种场以有趣方式共同相互作用形成的组合。所以你应该这样想象宇宙：它充满这些场，像流体一样的物质。12种物质场，4种力场。

cues.en: One of the matter fields starts to oscillate and ripple. Say the electron field starts to wave up and down, because there's electrons there. That will kick off one of the other fields. It will kick off, say, the electromagnetic field, which in turn will also oscillate and ripple. There'll be light, which is emitted.
cues.zh: 某种物质场开始振荡起伏。比如电子场开始上下波动，因为那里有电子。这会触发另一种场。比如它会激发由其引起的电磁场，电磁场接着也会振荡起伏。于是就会有光发射出来。

cues.en: At some point it will start interacting with the quark field, which in turn will oscillate and ripple. And the picture we end up with is this harmonious dance between all these fields interlocking each other, swaying, moving this way and that way. That's the picture that we have of the fundamental laws of physics.
cues.zh: 在某个时刻，它会开始与夸克场相互作用，夸克场反过来也会振荡起伏。我们最终看到的图景，就是所有这些场相互交织、此起彼伏、随之摆动的和谐共舞。这就是我们对物理学基本定律的认识。

cues.en: We have a theory which underlies all this. It is, to put it simply, the pinnacle of science. It's the greatest theory we've ever come up with. We've given it the most astonishingly rubbish name you've ever heard of. We call it the Standard Model. When you hear the name the Standard Model, it sounds tedious and mundane. It should really be replaced with the greatest theory in the history of human civilization. That's what we're looking at.
cues.zh: 我们有一套理论作为这一切的基石。简单来说，它是科学的巅峰。它是我们构想出最伟大的理论。但我们却给它起了一个你听过最不可思议的烂名字。我们称之为“标准模型”。当你听到“标准模型”这个名字时，感觉既乏味又平淡。它真该被改名为“人类文明史上最伟大的理论”。这就是我们所面对的理论。

cues.en: This is everything, except it's not quite. I've actually just missed out one field, this one extra thing we know about, which became quite famous in recent years. It was a field that was first suggested in the 1960s by a Scottish physicist called Peter Higgs. And it was, by the 1970s, it had become an integral part of the way we thought about the universe.
cues.zh: 这就是全部了，不过也不完全是。我其实刚漏掉了一个场，这是我们知道的额外一个场，它在近年来名声大噪。这个场最初是在 20 世纪 60 年代由一位名叫 Peter Higgs 的苏格兰物理学家提出的。到了 70 年代，它已经成为我们认识宇宙不可或缺的一部分。

cues.en: But for the longest time, we didn't have direct experimental evidence that this existed. Where direct experimental evidence means we make this Higgs field ripple, so we see a particle that's associated to it. And this changed. This changed famously four years ago at the LHC. These are the two experiments at the LHC that discovered it. They're sort of the size of cathedrals and just packed full of electronics. They're astonishing things. This is called ATLAS. This is called CMS.
cues.zh: 但在很长一段时间里，我们都没有直接的实验证据证明它的存在。所谓直接实验证据，就是让这个希格斯场产生涟漪，从而让我们看到与它相关的粒子。而这一局面被打破了。四年前，这一局面在 LHC 彻底改变，广为人知。这就是 LHC 发现它的两个实验装置。它们差不多有大教堂那么大，里面塞满了电子设备。真是令人惊叹的杰作。这个叫 ATLAS。这个叫 CMS。

cues.en: The Higgs particle doesn't last for long. The Higgs particle lasts about 10 to the minus 22 seconds. So it's not like you see it and you get to take a picture of it and put it on Instagram. It's a little more subtle. So this is the data, and this little bump here is how we know that this Higgs particle existed. This is a picture of Peter Higgs being found.
cues.zh: 希格斯粒子存在的时间并不长。希格斯粒子仅能存在约 10 的负 22 次方秒。所以并不是说你能亲眼看到它、拍张照然后发到 Instagram 上。它要更隐晦一些。这就是数据，而这个小突起就是我们知道希格斯粒子存在过的依据。这是一张 Peter Higgs 得知发现时的照片。

cues.en: So this was the final building block. You know, it was important. It was a really big deal, and it was important for two reasons. The first is that this is what's responsible for what we call mass in the universe. So the properties of all the particles, things like electric charge and mass, are really a statement about how their fields interact with other fields.
cues.zh: 所以这就是最后一块积木。你知道，它非常重要。这真是一件大事，其重要性体现在两方面。第一，它造就了我们在宇宙中所说的质量。所有粒子的性质，比如电荷和质量，实际上都是在描述它们的场是如何与其他场相互作用的。

cues.en: So the property that we call electric charge of an electron is a statement about how the electron field interacts with the electromagnetic field. And the property of its mass is the statement about how it interacts with the Higgs field. So understanding this was really needed so that we understand the meaning of mass in the universe. So it was a big deal. The other reason that it was a big deal is this was the final piece of our jigsaw.
cues.zh: 所以我们所说的电子电荷这一性质，其实是在描述电子场与电磁场是如何相互作用的。而它的质量性质，则是描述它与希格斯场是如何相互作用的。因此，弄清这一点对于我们理解宇宙中质量的含义至关重要。所以这是一件大事。而这之所以重要的另一个原因，在于它是我们这幅拼图的最后一块。

cues.en: We had this theory that we called the Standard Model. We've had it since the 1970s. This was the final thing that we needed to discover to be sure that this theory is correct. And the astonishing thing is this particle was predicted in the 1960s. 50 years we've been waiting. We finally created it in CERN. It behaves in exactly the way that we thought it would. Absolutely perfectly behaves as we predicted using these theories. OK.
cues.zh: 我们有一个被称为“标准模型”的理论。我们自1970年代起就拥有了它。这是我们需要发现的最后一环，以证实这个理论是正确的。令人惊叹的是，这种粒子早在1960年代就被预言了。我们等待了整整50年。我们终于在CERN创造出了它。它的表现与我们的预期完全一致。完全正如我们运用这些理论所预测的那样，分毫不差。好的。

cues.en: This is going to be the scary part of the talk. I've been telling you about this theory, and I've been waving my hands, pretending that I'm a field. Let me tell you what the theory really is. Let me just show you what we do. This is the equation for the standard model of physics. I don't expect you to understand it, not least because there are parts of this equation that no one on the planet understands.
cues.zh: 接下来的内容可能会有点吓人。我一直在给你们讲这个理论，一直在比手画脚，假装自己就是一个场。现在让我来告诉你们这个理论究竟是什么。让我向大家展示我们到底在做什么。这就是物理学标准模型的方程式。我并不指望大家能看懂，更何况这个方程式里的某些部分，全地球根本没有一个人能理解。

cues.en: But nonetheless, I want to show it to you for the following reason. This equation correctly predicts the result of every single experiment we've ever done in science. Everything is contained in this equation. This is really the pinnacle of the reductionist approach to science. It's all in here. So I'll admit, it's not the simplest equation in the world, but it's not the most complicated either.
cues.zh: 尽管如此，我之所以想给你们看，是因为以下这个原因。这个方程式准确地预测了我们科学界有史以来做过的每一个实验的结果。一切都包含在这个方程式中。这绝对是科学还原论方法的巅峰。全都在这里了。好吧，我承认它不是世界上最简单的方程式，但它也不是最复杂的。

cues.en: No, you can put it on a T-shirt if you want to. In fact, if you go to CERN, you can buy a T-shirt with this equation on it. Let me just give you a sense of what we're looking at. The first term here was written down by Albert Einstein and describes gravity. What that means is that if you can solve this tiny little part of the equation, just this R, you can, for example, predict how fast an apple falls from a tree.
cues.zh: 真的，你想把它印在T恤上都可以。事实上，如果你去CERN，就能买到印有这个方程式的T恤。让我先带大家大致感受一下我们看到的这些内容。这里的第一项是由Albert Einstein写下的，它描述了引力。这意味着，如果你能解开方程式中这小小的部分，仅仅这一个R，你就能预测，比如，一个苹果从树上掉下来的速度有多快。

cues.en: or the fact that the orbits of the planet around the sun form ellipses. Or you can predict what happens when two enormous black holes collide into each other and form a new black hole, sending out gravitational waves across the universe. Or in fact, you can predict how the entire universe itself expands. All of this comes from solving this little part of the equation. The next term in the equation was written down by James-Clark Maxwell, and it tells you everything about electromagnetism.
cues.zh: 或者行星绕太阳运行的轨道呈椭圆形这一事实。或者你能够预测，当两个巨大的黑洞相互碰撞并形成一个新黑洞时会发生什么，向整个宇宙辐射出引力波。又或者说，你其实可以预测整个宇宙自身是如何膨胀的。这一切都源于解开这个方程式中如此微小的部分。方程式中的下一项是由James-Clark Maxwell写下的，它揭示了关于电磁学的一切。

cues.en: So all the experiments that Faraday spent a lifetime doing in this building, in fact, all the experiments over many centuries, from Coulomb to Faraday to Hertz to modern developments of lasers, everything in this tiny little part of...
cues.zh: 因此，法拉第在这栋楼里用尽一生所做的全部实验，事实上，几个世纪以来从库仑、法拉第、赫兹到现代激光技术的所有实验，全部都囊括在这个微小局部的……

cues.en: of the equation. So there's some power in these equations. This is the equation that governs the strong nuclear force, the weak nuclear force. This is an equation that was first written down by a British physicist called Paul Dirac. It describes the matter, describes those 12 particles that make up the matter. Astonishingly, each of them obeys exactly the same equation. These are the equations of Peter Higgs, and this is an equation that tells you how the matter interacts with the Higgs particle.
cues.zh: ……方程之中。所以这些方程蕴含着巨大的力量。这个方程主导着强核力和弱核力。而这个方程最初是由一位名叫 Paul Dirac 的英国物理学家写下的。它描述了物质，描述了构成物质的那 12 种粒子。令人惊叹的是，它们每一种都完全遵循着同一个方程。这些是 Peter Higgs 的方程，而这个方程则揭示了物质是如何与希格斯粒子相互作用的。

cues.en: So everything is in here. It's really an astonishing achievement. This is our current limit of knowledge. We've never done an experiment that cannot be explained by this equation, and we've never found a way in which this equation stops working. So this is the best thing that we currently have. OK. It's the best thing that we currently have, however, we want to do better. Because we know for sure that there's stuff out there that is not...
cues.zh: 所以万物尽在其中。这真是一项惊人的成就。这就是我们目前认知的极限。我们从未做过任何一个无法用这个方程解释的实验，我们也从未发现这个方程在何种情况下会失效。所以这就是我们目前所拥有的巅峰之作。好的。虽然这是我们目前的最高成就，但我们还想做得更好。因为我们确信，外面还有一些东西是无法……

cues.en: explained by this. And the reason we know is that although this explains every single experiment we've ever done here on Earth, if we look out into the sky, there's extra stuff which is still a mystery. So if we look out into space, there are, for example, invisible particles out there. In fact, there's many more invisible particles than there are visible particles. We call them dark matter. We can't see them.
cues.zh: ……被它所解释的。我们之所以知道这一点，是因为尽管它解释了我们在地球上做过的每一个实验，但如果我们抬头仰望星空，就会发现仍有许多谜团无法解释。比如当我们望向太空，那里存在着看不见的粒子。事实上，隐形粒子的数量远比可见粒子要多得多。我们称之为暗物质。我们看不见它们。

cues.en: obviously, because they're invisible, but we can see their effects. We can see their effects on the way galaxies rotate or the way they bend light around galaxies. They're out there. We don't know what they are. There's even more mysterious things. There's something called dark energy, which is spread throughout all of space. It's also some kind of field, although not one we understand, that's causing everything in the universe to repel everything else. Other things. We know that early in the first few seconds,
cues.zh: 这显而易见，因为它们是隐形的，但我们能看到它们的影响。我们能看到它们对星系旋转方式的影响，或是它们如何使星系周围的光线发生弯曲。它们确实存在，但我们不知道它们究竟是什么。还有更神秘的东西。有一种叫做暗能量的存在，它弥漫在整个空间中。它也是某种场，尽管我们还不了解它，它正在导致宇宙中的一切事物彼此排斥。还有其他事情。我们知道在宇宙诞生的最初几秒内，

cues.en: Earlier than that, the first few fractions of a second after the Big Bang, the universe underwent a very rapid phase of expansion that we call inflation. We know it happened, but it's not explained by that equation that I just showed you. So these are the kind of things that we're going to have to understand if we're going to move forward and decide what the next laws of physics are that go beyond the standard model.
cues.zh: 甚至比那还要早，在大爆炸后的最初极小零点几秒内，宇宙经历了一个极其快速的膨胀阶段，我们称之为暴胀。我们知道它发生过，但刚才我展示的那个方程却无法解释它。所以，如果我们想要向前迈进，确定超越标准模型的下一代物理定律是什么，这些就是我们必须要去理解的问题。

cues.en: I could spend hours talking about either of these. I'm going to focus just on the last one. I'm going to tell you a little bit about inflation. So the universe is 13.8 billion years old. And we understand fairly well, well, we don't understand at all how it started. We don't understand what kicked it all off at time t equals zero. But we understand fairly well what happened after it started. And we know in particular that for the first...
cues.zh: 关于这两者中的任何一个，我都能讲上好几个小时。但我只打算聚焦在最后一个上。我想跟大家聊聊宇宙暴胀。宇宙已经有138亿年的历史了。我们相当清楚——好吧，其实我们完全不知道它是怎么开始的。我们不知道在时间 t 等于零时，究竟是什么引发了一切。但我们相当清楚它开始之后发生了什么。我们尤其清楚的是，在最初的……

cues.en: the first 380,000 years of the universe, it was filled with a fireball. And we know this for sure because we've seen the fireball. In fact, we've seen it and we've taken a photograph of it. This is called the cosmic microwave background radiation, but a much better name for it is the fireball that filled the universe when it was much younger. The fireball...
cues.zh: 在宇宙最初的38万年里，它充斥着一个大火球。我们之所以确信这一点，是因为我们观测到了这个火球。事实上，我们不仅看到了，还拍下了照片。这被称为宇宙微波背景辐射，但一个更贴切的名字是：在宇宙年轻得多时充斥其中的大火球。这个火球……

cues.en: cooled down, its light has been streaming through the universe for 13.8 billion years, but we can see it, we can take this photograph of it, and we can sort of understand very well what was happening in these first few moments of the universe. And you can see it. It looks literally like a fireball. There's red bits that are hotter, there's blue bits that are colder. And by studying this flickering that you can see in this picture, we get a lot of information about what was going on back 13.8.
cues.zh: 冷却了下来，它的光芒在宇宙中穿行了138亿年，但我们依然能看到它，能拍下这张照片，而且某种程度上，我们能非常透彻地理解宇宙最初那些时刻发生了什么。大家可以看到它。它看起来真就跟个大火球一样。红色的部分温度更高，蓝色的部分温度更低。通过研究大家在图中看到的这些微小闪烁起伏，我们获得了大量关于138亿年前的信息，

cues.en: billion years ago when the universe was a baby. One of the main questions we want to ask is what caused the flickering in the fireball? And we have an answer to this. We have an answer which I think is one of the most astonishing things in all of science. It turns out that although the fireball lasted for 380,000 years, whatever caused this flickering could not have taken place during the vast majority of that time.
cues.zh: 也就是宇宙尚在婴儿期时的信息。我们想问的核心问题之一是：到底是什么引起了火球中的这种起伏闪烁？对此我们已有答案。这个答案在我看来是整个科学界最令人惊叹的事情之一。事实证明，尽管大火球持续了38万年之久，但无论引发这种闪烁起伏的是什么，它都不可能发生在这段漫长时光的大部分阶段里。

cues.en: whatever caused the flickering in this fireball actually took place in the first few very fractions of a second after the Big Bang. And what it was was the following. So when the universe was very, very young, soon after the Big Bang, there were no particles, but there were quantum fields, because the quantum fields were everywhere.
cues.zh: 引发这个大火球微小起伏的诱因，实际上发生在宇宙大爆炸后短短的一刹那之间。事情的经过是这样的。在宇宙极度年轻、也就是大爆炸后不久，那时还没有任何粒子，但存在着量子场，因为量子场无处不在。

cues.en: and there were these quantum vacuum fluctuations. And what happened was the universe expanded very, very quickly, and it caught these quantum fluctuations in the act. So the quantum fluctuations were stretched across the entire sky, where they became frozen, and it's these vacuum fluctuations here, which are the ripples that you see in the fireball.
cues.zh: 并且存在着这些量子真空涨落。接着发生的事情是，宇宙以极快的速度急剧膨胀，当场捕获了这些量子涨落。于是量子涨落被拉伸到了整个天空，并在那里冻结了下来，正是这里的这些真空涨落，演变成了大家在火球中所看到的涟漪起伏。

cues.en: So it's an astonishing story. The quantum vacuum fluctuations were taking place 10 to the minus 30 seconds after the Big Bang. They were absolutely microscopic. And now we see them stretched across the entire universe, stretched 20 billion light years across the sky. That's what you're seeing here. And yet, you do the calculations for this, and it batches perfectly what you see here. So this is another of the great triumphs of...
cues.zh: 所以这是一个令人惊叹的故事。量子真空涨落发生在大爆炸后10的负30次方秒。它们绝对是微观层面的。而如今我们看到它们被拉伸到了整个宇宙，横跨天际达200亿光年之遥。这就是大家眼前所看到的景象。然而，当你对此进行理论计算时，它与你在这里看到的景象完美吻合。所以，这是……的又一次伟大胜利。

cues.en: of quantum field theory. But it leaves lots of questions. The most important one is, which field are we seeing here? Which field is this that's imprinted on the background radiation? And the answer is we don't know. The only one of the standard model fields it has a hope of being is the Higgs, but most of us think it's not the Higgs, but probably something new. But what we'd like to do moving forward into the future is get a much better picture of this fireball. In particular, get the polarization of the light,
cues.zh: 量子场论的成果。但它留下了很多疑问。最关键的问题是，我们在这里看到的究竟是哪个场？印在背景辐射上的究竟是哪种场？答案是我们不知道。在标准模型的场中，唯一有希望的是希格斯场，但我们大多数人认为它不是希格斯场，而很可能是某种新东西。不过，展望未来，我们想做的是获得这团火球更清晰的图像。特别是获取光的偏振，

cues.en: And by getting a picture of this, we can understand much better the properties of this field that was fluctuating in the early universe. OK, this, looking forward, is one of the best hopes that we have for going beyond the standard model and understanding new physics. In the last 10 minutes, though, I'd like to bring you back down to Earth. Sort of. We've got lots of experiments here on Earth.
cues.zh: 通过获取这样的图像，我们就能更好地理解早期宇宙中这一波动场的性质。好的，展望未来，这是我们超越标准模型并理解新物理学的最大希望之一。不过在最后10分钟里，我想带大家回到地球。某种程度上算是吧。我们在地球上做了很多实验，

cues.en: where we're also trying to do better, where we're also trying to go beyond the standard model of physics, beyond that equation, to understand what's new. And there's many of them, but the most prominent is the one I've already mentioned. It's the LHC. So what happened was the LHC discovered the Higgs boson in 2012.
cues.zh: 我们也在尝试做得更好，尝试超越物理学的标准模型，超越那个方程，去理解有什么新发现。这样的实验有很多，但最著名的就是我刚才提到的那个，也就是 LHC。情况是这样的，LHC 在2012年发现了希格斯玻色子。

cues.en: And soon afterwards, it closed down for two years. It had an upgrade. And last year, in 2015, the LHC turned on again with twice the energy that it had when it discovered the Higgs. And the goal was twofold. The goal was, firstly, to understand the Higgs better, which is done fantastically, and secondly, to discover new physics that lies beyond the Higgs, new physics beyond the standard model.
cues.zh: 不久之后，它关机停运了两年。它进行了升级。而在去年，也就是2015年，LHC 重新启动，能量达到了发现希格斯粒子时的两倍。目标有两个：首先是更好地了解希格斯粒子，这一点完成得非常出色；其次是发现超越希格斯粒子的新物理，也就是超越标准模型的新物理。

cues.en: So before I tell you what it's seen, let me tell you some of the ideas we had, some of our expectations and hopes for what would happen moving forward. So this is our favorite equation again. The idea has always been the following. If you're a Victorian scientist and you go back and you look at the periodic table of elements, then it's true that there's patterns in there that give a hint
cues.zh: 在告诉大家它看到了什么之前，让我先讲讲我们之前的一些想法，以及我们对未来的期待与希望。这又是我们最喜欢的方程。思路一直都是这样的。如果你是维多利亚时代的科学家，回头去看元素周期表，里面确实存在某些规律，能给出一些线索，

cues.en: of the structure that lies underneath. There's numbers that repeat themselves. Where if you're very smart, you might start to realize that, yes, there is something deeper than just these elements. So our hope as theorists is to look at this equation and see if maybe we can just find patterns in this equation that suggest there might be something deeper that lies underneath. And they're there.
cues.zh: 暗示着其背后的潜在结构。里面有些数字会重复出现。如果你非常聪明，可能就会开始意识到，是的，除了这些元素之外，确实存在着更深层的东西。所以我们作为理论物理学家的希望，就是审视这个方程，看看能否在其中找到某些规律，表明可能存在着更深层次的东西。而它们确实存在。

cues.en: So let me give you an example. This is the equation that describes the force of electricity and magnetism. And it's almost the same as the equations which describe the forces for the strong force and the weak nuclear force. In fact, you can see, I've just changed letters. It's a little more complicated than that, but it's not much more complicated. The three forces really look similar. So you might wonder, well,
cues.zh: 让我给你们举个例子。这是描述电磁力的方程。它和描述强力以及弱核力的方程几乎一模一样。事实上，你们能看出来，我只是改了字母而已。实际情况要比这稍微复杂一点，但并没有复杂多少。这三种力看起来真的很相似。所以你可能会想，嗯，

cues.en: Maybe there's not three forces in the universe. Maybe those three forces are actually just one force, and when we think there's three forces, it's because we're looking at that one force just from slightly different perspectives. Maybe. Here's something else which is amazing. These are the equations for the 12 matter fields in the universe, the neutrinos, the electrons and the quarks. Each of them obeys exactly the same equation. Each of them obeys the Dirac equation.
cues.zh: 也许宇宙中并没有三种力。也许这三种力实际上只是一种力，而我们之所以认为有三种力，是因为我们只是从稍微不同的角度看待同一种力。也许吧。还有一件更神奇的事。这些是描述宇宙中12种物质场的方程，中微子、电子和夸克。它们每一个都遵循完全相同的方程。每一个都遵循狄拉克方程。

cues.en: So, again, you might wonder that, well, maybe there are 12 different fields, maybe they're all the same field and the same particle, and the fact they look different is, again, maybe just because we're looking at them from slightly different perspectives. Maybe. So, these ideas that I've been suggesting go by the name of unification. The idea that the three forces are actually combined into one is what's called grand unification.
cues.zh: 所以，你可能又会想，也许这12种不同的场，其实都是同一种场、同一种粒子，它们看起来不同，也可能只是因为我们观察的角度略有不同。也许吧。我刚才提到的这些想法，被称为“统一”。而认为这三种力其实合而为一的想法，就被称为“大一统”。

cues.en: And it's very easy. It's very easy to write down a mathematical theory in which all of these are just one force which appears to be three from our perspective. There are other possibilities here. You might say, well, this is the matter and these are the forces, and the equations are different, but they're not that different, because ultimately they're both just fields.
cues.zh: 而且这很容易。要写出一个数学理论，让所有这些力都归为一种力，只是在我们看来像是三种，其实非常容易。这里还有其他可能性。你可能会说，这些是物质，那些是力，它们的方程虽然不同，但也差得不多，因为归根结底它们都只是场。

cues.en: So you might wonder if maybe there's some way in which the matter and the forces are related to each other Well, we have a theory for that as well. It's a theory that's called supersymmetry and It's a beautiful theory. It's very deep conceptually And it sort of you know smells like it might be right Finally, you might be really really bold you might say well
cues.zh: 所以你可能会想，物质和力之间是否也存在某种关联？对此我们同样有一套理论。这个理论叫作“超对称”，它是一个非常优美的理论。在概念上极其深刻，而且感觉上……怎么说呢，感觉它很有可能是对的。最后，你还可以更大胆一点，你可以说：

cues.en: Can I just combine the lot? Can I just get rid of all of these terms and just write down one single term from which everything else emerges? Gravity, the forces, the particles, the Higgs, everything. Well, I've got something for you if you want that as well. It's called string theory. So we have a possibility for a theory which contains all of this in one simple concept.
cues.zh: 我能不能把这一切全部结合起来？能不能把所有这些项统统扔掉，只写出一个项，然后万物皆由它演化而来？包括引力、各种力、粒子、Higgs玻色子，所有的一切。如果你想这样，我也能满足你。它叫作“弦理论”。所以我们确实有可能得到一个理论，用一个简单的概念包揽这一切。

cues.en: And the question going forward, of course, is, are these right? It's very easy for us theorists to have these ideas. And I should say, these ideas of what's driven theoretical physics for 30 years, but we want to know, are they right? And we've got a way of telling they're right. We do experiments. So I should say, if you want to know if string theory is right, we don't have any way to test it at the moment. But if you want to know if some of these other ideas are right, then that's what the LHC should be doing.
cues.zh: 接下来要问的当然是：这些是对的吗？对于我们理论学家来说，想出这些点子太容易了。我得说，正是这些想法推动了理论物理学30年的发展，但我们想知道的是：它们对吗？而我们有办法知道答案，那就是做实验。所以我得说，如果你想知道弦理论对不对，我们目前还没有任何检验的方法。但如果你想知道其他这些想法对不对，那正是LHC该做的事。

cues.en: The reason that we built the LHC was firstly to find the Higgs. OK, it worked. And secondly, to test these kind of ideas that we've been having to see what lies beyond. So the LHC has been running. It's been running for two years. It's been running like an absolute dream. It's just a perfect machine. Two years, this is what it's seen. Absolutely nothing. All of these fantastic, beautiful ideas that we've had, none of them are showing up at all.
cues.zh: 我们建造LHC，首先是为了寻找Higgs粒子。好的，这成了。其次，是为了检验我们提出来的这些想法，去看看未知领域还有什么。于是LHC一直在运行。它已经运行了两年。运行状态简直如同梦幻一般，完全是一台完美的机器。两年来，它看到了什么呢？什么都没看到。我们提出过的所有这些精妙、优美的想法，全都没有出现。

cues.en: And the question going forward is, what are we going to do about it? How are we going to make progress in understanding the next layer of physics when the LHC isn't seeing anything and our ideas just don't appear to be the way that nature works? I should tell you often, I don't have a good answer to this. My impression is that most of my community is a little bit shell-shocked by what happened.
cues.zh: 那么接下来的问题是，我们该怎么办？当 LHC 什么都没发现，而我们的想法似乎又与大自然的运作方式不符时，我们该如何在理解物理学的下一层面上取得进展？坦白说，我并没有一个好答案。我的感觉是，圈内大多数人对发生的一切都有些发懵。

cues.en: There's certainly no consensus in the community to move forward, but I think there's three responses that the sort of various people have had that I'd like to share with you. I think all three of these responses are reasonable up to a point. The first response to the LHC not seeing anything is the following.
cues.zh: 学术界在下一步该怎么走上显然没有共识，但我觉得有三种不同人的应对态度，我想和大家分享一下。我认为这三种态度在某种程度上都讲得通。对 LHC 一无所获的第一种回应是这样的。

cues.en: Well, you young kids, you're so pessimistic, it's all doom and gloom with you. You just need a little bit more patience. You know, it didn't see anything last year and it didn't see anything this year, but next year it's going to see something. And if not next year, it's the year after that that it's going to see something. It's usually my very illustrious senior colleagues that have this response. And you know what? They could easily be right. It could easily be that next year the LHC discovers something astonishing and it sets us on the path to understanding the next layer of reality.
cues.zh: “哎呀，你们这帮年轻人太悲观了，整天觉得大难临头。你们只需要再多点耐心。你看，虽然它去年没发现什么，今年也没发现什么，但明年肯定能有新发现。即使明年没有，后年也一定会有。”这种回应通常来自我那些德高望重的前辈同行。你猜怎么着？他们很可能是对的。说不定明年 LHC 就会有惊人发现，引领我们去理解现实世界的下一层本质。

cues.en: But it's also true that these same people were predicting that it would have seen something by now. And it's also true that this can't keep going for much longer. If the LHC doesn't see something within, say, a two-year timescale, it seems very, very unlikely that it's going to see something moving forward. It's possible. It just seems unlikely. So we'll know. I hope with all my heart that the LHC discovers something next year or the year after.
cues.zh: 但同样事实是，正是这帮人曾经预言它现在早就该有所发现了。而且，这种情况也不可能一直持续下去。如果 LHC 在比如两年的时间跨度内什么都没发现，那以后再有新发现的希望就非常非常渺茫了。不是完全不可能，只是希望很渺茫。所以我们很快就会知道结果。我打心底里希望 LHC 明年或后年能有所突破。

cues.en: But I think we have to prepare for the worst, that maybe it won't. OK, response number two. Response number two, which is sort of altered by similar people. Well, all our theories are so beautiful, they absolutely have to be correct, and what we really need is a bigger machine. Ten times bigger, we'll do it. OK, again, they might be right. I don't have a good argument against it. The obvious rebuttal, however, is that a new machine costs $10 billion.
cues.zh: 但我认为我们必须做最坏的打算，那就是它可能依然一无所获。好，第二种回应。第二种回应往往也出自同一批人：“既然我们的理论都如此优美，它们就绝不可能错，我们真正需要的是一台更大的机器。只要大上十倍，就足够了。”好，他们可能依然是对的，我提不出什么有力的反驳。然而显而易见的反驳在于，一台新机器要耗资 100 亿美元。

cues.en: And there's not too many governments in the world that have $10 billion to spare for us to explore these ideas. There's one. The one is China.
cues.zh: 而世界上并没有多少国家政府手头有 100 亿美元的闲钱，来供我们探索这些想法。有一个国家有，那就是中国。

cues.en: And so if this machine is going to be built at all, it's going to be built by the Chinese government. I think the Chinese government would see it as extremely attractive if the whole community of particle physicists and engineers that are currently based in CERN in Geneva move to a town that's slightly north of Beijing. I think they'd view that as a political and economic gain, and there's a real chance that they may decide to build this machine. If they do, it's about 20 years for it to be built. So we're waiting slightly longer.
cues.zh: 所以如果这台机器真能建起来，那也只能由中国政府来建。我认为中国政府会觉得这极具吸引力，如果目前常驻日内瓦 CERN 的整个粒子物理学家和工程师群体，都能搬到北京以北的一座小镇上。我认为他们会把这视为政治和经济上的双赢，而且他们真的很有可能会决定建造这台机器。如果真建的话，大约需要 20 年才能建成，所以我们还得再多等一段时间。

cues.en: There's a third response, and I should say the third response is kind of the camp I'm in. I should mention up front, it's speculative and it's probably not endorsed by most of my peers. So this is really just my personal opinion at this point. This is my take on this. This is the equation that we know is right.
cues.zh: 还有第三种回应，我得说我自己大概就属于这个阵营。首先要说明的是，这只是推测，同行里大概多数人并不认同。所以眼下这纯粹是我个人的看法，这是我对此的理解。这个方程，我们已知它是正确的。

cues.en: This is sort of the bedrock of our understanding. But although we know it's right, there's an awful lot in this equation that we haven't understood. There's an awful lot to me that's still mysterious in this equation. So although this equation looked like there were suggestions of unification, maybe they're just red herrings. And maybe if we just work harder on trying to understand this equation more,
cues.zh: 这可以说是我们理解的基石。但尽管我们知道它是对的，这个方程里依然有大量我们未能理解的东西。在我看来，这里面至今仍有太多谜团。因此，尽管这个方程看似暗示着大一统，但也可能只是些障眼法。也许只要我们再下点苦功，去更深入地理解这个方程，

cues.en: we'll find that there are other patterns that emerge. So my response is, I think that maybe we should just go back to the drawing board and start to challenge some of the assumptions and paradigms that we've been holding for the past 30 years. So I should admit, I feel quite energized, actually, by the lack of results for the LHC. It feels good to me that everyone was wrong. It's when we're wrong that we start to make progress.
cues.zh: 就会发现浮现出其他的模式。所以我的回应是，我觉得也许我们该推倒重来，开始去质疑过去30年里我们一直坚信的某些假设和范式。我得承认，LHC 没有探测到预期结果，其实让我感到相当振奋。大家都猜错了，这让我觉得挺棒的。因为只有在我们犯错的时候，我们才开始取得进展。

cues.en: So I sort of feel quite happy about this and think that there's a very real chance that we could just start thinking about different ideas.
cues.zh: 所以我对此感到挺高兴的，并且认为我们完全有可能开始去思考截然不同的想法了。

cues.en: There are hints in here, there are hints to me about mathematical patterns that we haven't explored. There's hints in this about connections to other areas of science, things like condensed matter physics, which is the science of how materials work, or quantum information science, which is the attempt to build a quantum computer. All of these fantastic subjects have new ideas which sort of feed in to the kind of questions that we're asking here.
cues.zh: 这里面其实有提示，在我看来，这里暗示着我们尚未探索的数学规律。这里也暗示着与其他科学领域的联系，比如凝聚态物理——也就是研究材料机制的科学，或者是量子信息科学——也就是尝试建造量子计算机的学科。所有这些精彩的领域所孕育的新想法，都在反哺我们这里所探讨的各类问题。

cues.en: So I'm quite optimistic that moving forward, we can make progress. Maybe not the progress that we thought we'd make a few years ago, but just something new. So that's the punchline of my talk. The punchline is that this is the single greatest equation that we've ever written down. But I hope that someday we can give you something better. Thank you for your attention. There's nothing discreet about the Schrödinger equation.
cues.zh: 所以我非常乐观，相信未来我们能取得突破。也许不是几年前我们预期的那种进展，但必定会是些全新的东西。这就是我演讲的核心结论。结论就是：这是人类有史以来写下的最伟大的方程。但我希望有一天，我们能为大家呈现出更好的东西。感谢大家的聆听。薛定谔方程中没有任何离散的成分。

cues.en: The Schrödinger equation is something to do with a smooth field like wave function. The discreteness is something which emerges when you solve the Schrödinger equation. So it's not built into the heart of nature.
cues.zh: 薛定谔方程探讨的是平滑场般的波函数。离散性只是你在求解薛定谔方程时所涌现出来的特性。所以它并非自然界内在的核心本质。
